writingIdeas.viewpoint: Clothing durability should be easier to assess.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Consumers cannot make sustainable choices when information about garment quality is hidden.
writingIdeas.argument: Online photographs reveal colour and style but say little about stitching, fabric weight or repair. As a result, shoppers may choose a cheaper garment that loses shape after a few washes. Clear construction details and realistic care information would support better comparison. Brands that make durable clothes could compete on quality rather than constant novelty. Better information would reduce replacement costs and unnecessary textile waste.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: School dress codes should focus on function and fairness.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Clothing rules are legitimate when they support safety and learning rather than enforce narrow tastes.
writingIdeas.argument: A basic uniform can reduce competition over expensive brands and make preparation simpler. Rules become problematic when they target one gender more heavily or punish harmless cultural styles. Students also need clothing suitable for weather and physical activity. Schools should explain the practical purpose of each requirement and consult families about cost. A fair dress code is clear, affordable and consistently applied.

speaking.question: Do you enjoy buying clothes?
speaking.answer: Only when I know what I need. I find browsing without a purpose tiring because there are too many similar choices. I normally replace an item that has worn out and look for something comfortable that works with clothes I already own. Finding the right fit is more satisfying to me than following a new trend.

speaking.question: Do you wear different clothes for work and your free time?
speaking.answer: Yes, although the difference isn’t dramatic. For work I wear simple shirts, trousers and fairly formal shoes because they look neat on video calls and in meetings. In my free time I choose softer fabrics and trainers. Having that change also helps me feel that the working day has ended when I get home.

reading.title: What a Label Cannot Tell You
paragraphs: A clothing label can identify fibre content, country of manufacture and washing instructions. These facts are useful, but they do not reveal how long the garment will last. Two shirts made from the same percentage of cotton may perform differently because of fibre length, fabric density, stitching and finishing. Durability is produced by construction, not by a single material name.

Consumers often judge quality through price or brand reputation. Both can provide clues, yet neither is reliable. A high price may reflect advertising, a central shop location or limited production rather than stronger fabric. Meanwhile, an inexpensive garment can wear well if its design is simple and the seams are secure. The difficulty is that many weaknesses appear only after repeated washing.

Care also changes lifespan. Heat, aggressive detergent and unnecessary washing place stress on fibres and colour. Repairing a loose button or small tear can prevent greater damage, but modern garments are not always designed for easy repair. Decorative linings may hide seams, and replacement fasteners can be difficult to match. Skills once common in households have also become less widespread.

A meaningful durability label would need standard tests, such as resistance to rubbing, colour loss and seam failure. It would still be an estimate because wear depends on use and care. Nevertheless, comparable information could shift attention from the purchase price to cost per use. The most sustainable garment is not automatically the one with a particular fibre; it is often the one that remains useful and is worn repeatedly.

Rental and resale markets offer another source of durability evidence. A garment that retains shape and colour can circulate through several owners, spreading its production impact across more uses. However, second-hand trade cannot correct extremely weak construction: if an item fails quickly, there is nothing useful to pass on. Longevity must begin when the garment is designed.
